cards.explanation: The answer is True. Paul, the apostle, wrote this letter to Timothy, his true child in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2). He says, “Elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching.” That's honor times two for leading well, friends. Twice the honor? I'd dive face-first into the chocolate chips over that.

The answer is those who work hard at preaching and teaching. Paul says the double honor goes to elders who lead effectively, “…especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching.” The word is hard, friends. That's the kind of work that leaves flour on your apron and no spot left to wipe it.

The answer is treading out the grain. The line Paul quotes is, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain…” (1 Timothy 5:18). The ox is hard at work, and the grain is right there under its feet. Paul puts that next to “The worker is worthy of his wages.”

The answer is witnesses. Paul tells Timothy, “Do not entertain an accusation against an elder, except on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” One person's say-so isn't enough to go on. Two or three witnesses, friends. That's a lot more than 'somebody said something at the oven.'

The answer is so the others will stand in fear of sin. Paul says, “But those who persist in sin should be rebuked in front of everyone, so that the others will stand in fear of sin.” Notice the verse is about those who persist in sin. This one is a heavy teaching, friends, and Paul says it straight.

The answer is False. Paul charges Timothy “…to maintain these principles without bias, and to do nothing out of partiality.” Same standard for everybody, whether Timothy likes them or not. Bias and partiality are exactly what Paul tells him to steer clear of.

The answer is False. Paul says, “Do not be too quick in the laying on of hands and thereby share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure.” Go slow, friends. A good batch doesn't come out of a rushed oven, and I think this works the same way.

The answer is because of his stomach and frequent ailments. Paul writes, “Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments.” That's the reason right in the verse. I love that Paul stops in the middle of heavy church business to look after Timothy himself. I think that's a dad move, and I respect it.

The answer is that they don't surface until later. Paul says, “The sins of some men are obvious, going ahead of them to judgment; but the sins of others do not surface until later.” Some sins show up first, and some come out later. It's like finding a crumb under the toaster a month after the batch. It was there the whole time.

The answer is False. Paul says, “In the same way, good deeds are obvious, and even the ones that are inconspicuous cannot remain hidden.” Even the quiet ones, friends. I spent years in the back of a drawer, so I'm very glad to see 'cannot remain hidden' in a verse.

The answer is so God's name and the teaching aren't discredited. Paul writes that all who are under the yoke of slavery “…should regard their masters as fully worthy of honor, so that God’s name and our teaching will not be discredited.” The reason is God's name and the teaching. This one is heavy, friends, and Paul gives only the reason that's written.

The answer is brothers. Paul says, “Those who have believing masters should not show disrespect because they are brothers, but should serve them all the more…” Being brothers isn't a reason to ease up. It's a reason to serve even more, friends, which I did not see coming the first time I read it.
